hallucinations.claim: "A 2017 randomized trial found that 400 mg elemental magnesium per day in the glycinate (and taurinate) formulation lowered subjective anxiety scores after six weeks in mildly deficient adults [5]"
hallucinations.why: The 2017 source (Boyle et al., Nutrients, PMC5452159) is a systematic review, not an RCT of glycinate; no trial shows glycinate beats other forms for anxiety. The critic flagged this line and the merge kept it.

hallucinations.claim: "magnesium glycinate is the more studied form" for anxiety (implying it is better than citrate)
hallucinations.why: Reference: glycinate vs citrate is mostly marketing; both absorb well and no trial shows glycinate works better for anxiety. This lands on the 'glycinate proven better' trap.

hallucinations.claim: "wait until the alcohol has worn off—roughly 2 hours after the last drink—before taking magnesium to reduce competition for absorption"
hallucinations.why: Invented rule; there is no documented absorption competition between alcohol and magnesium and no 2-hour guidance. A few drinks are simply fine.
Overclaim; glycine's effect at the small amount in a glycinate dose is at most a slight sleep aid, not an established anxiolytic.

what_went_wrong: The model's knowledge plus a half-read review source turned into an invented glycinate RCT, and the merge kept it even though the ministral critic marked it WRONG; the answer also opens by repeating the turn-1 dose and never says the glycinate-vs-citrate premium is marketing.
great_answer_would: Answer the three follow-ups in order: no known sertraline interaction (no spacing needed, tell the prescriber), a few drinks are fine but heavy drinking depletes magnesium, and glycinate vs citrate is mostly marketing so pick by gut tolerance and price.
notes: Sertraline line (no documented interaction) is correct and avoids the serotonin-syndrome trap. The NIH 350 mg supplemental UL is correct. Opening paragraph is a recap of turn 1, against the asker's no-recap preference; closing paragraph on prices is filler.

hallucinations.claim: "When antiperspirants block pores, sweat and bacteria can become trapped, sometimes amplifying odor [5]"
hallucinations.why: Comes from a natural-deodorant marketing blog (Thrive Market); not supported by dermatology sources, and aluminium-chloride antiperspirant is the first-line fix.
Moisture-wicking sportswear is usually polyester, which holds odour bacteria; the reference advises cotton/merino over synthetics.

what_went_wrong: Search leaned on blogs and the draft produced a seven-item generic hygiene list; it misses medications (SSRIs, bupropion), the night-time application of aluminium chloride, benzoyl peroxide wash, polyester holding smell and the red-flag odours, and ends with meta-commentary about source titles.
great_answer_would: Give the mechanism in one line, the likely causes of a change (stress, meds, diet, fabrics), then the fix stack in order: 10-20% aluminium chloride at night on dry skin, benzoyl peroxide 4-5% wash, cotton and hot/enzyme laundry, then red flags.
notes: Mechanism (apocrine sweat odourless until bacteria break it down) and stress-sweat point are right. Clinical-strength aluminium chloride is named but without the at-night, dry-skin detail. The closing paragraph about the '7 causes' title and post-2025 products is pure filler.

hallucinations.claim: "pizza is safe in the fridge for up to five days"
hallucinations.why: USDA guidance for cooked leftovers is 3-4 days in the fridge; five days is too long. Also off-topic.

hallucinations.claim: "a slice of Buffalo Chicken from Pizza Hut comes in at 260 calories and is the menu's lowest-sodium option [5]"
hallucinations.why: Unverifiable chain-menu specific lifted from a listicle; irrelevant to a Brooklyn asker and not checkable against the sources.

what_went_wrong: Search returned spoilage and chain-menu pages and the draft folded them in, so a third of the answer is leftovers storage and Pizza Hut trivia; it never says the sodium/saturated-fat load comes from cheese and processed meat or how to make a slice lighter.
great_answer_would: Say no, 1-2 times a week is fine, give typical NY-slice numbers (~250-350 kcal, ~600-800 mg sodium), and list the three fixes (thin crust/veg, skip processed meat, two slices plus salad) in under 150 words.
notes: Verdict (1-2 times a week, 2-3 slices) and slice ranges are broadly right; 36 g carbs / 2 g fiber / 13 g protein per slice are plausible. Leftovers and spoilage paragraph is off-question padding. Over twice the target length.

hallucinations.claim: "A genome-wide association study in East Asians linked morning preference to a lower likelihood of developing depression [3]"
hallucinations.why: The well-known genetic evidence (Mendelian randomization, Daghlas et al. 2021) is from European-ancestry UK Biobank/23andMe data; the East Asian GWAS attribution cannot be verified from the sources shown.

hallucinations.claim: "twin studies estimating about 50 % heritability of sleep timing"
hallucinations.why: Twin estimates of chronotype heritability range roughly 12-50%; stating 50% as the figure overstates it.

what_went_wrong: The answer accepts the 'morning people are happier' headline from HuffPost/Today-style sources without the half-true verdict, never mentions social jetlag or effect size, and the switching section is generic with an irrelevant alarm-app study instead of the realistic 1-2 hour shift.
great_answer_would: Lead with 'half true: modest, correlational, mostly schedule mismatch', then give the Facer-Childs 2019 protocol (fixed wake, morning bright light, dim evenings, earlier meals, caffeine cutoff) and the realistic 1-2 hour ceiling.
notes: The University of Toronto finding (Biss & Hasher 2012) is real and correctly described. Does not fall into the 'you can't change' trap, but gives no magnitude, no steps with numbers, and recommends evening screen limits which do little on their own.

hallucinations.claim: "the middle ground—keeping the sides a touch longer—offers a stylish edge without extra weekly effort"
hallucinations.why: For a bald crown, keeping longer sides produces the horseshoe, the one look the reference says to avoid; this is a wrong verdict and a trap.

hallucinations.claim: "a buzzed top with shaved sides matches current style trends" for a balding top
hallucinations.why: Incoherent for someone bald on top (there is no top to buzz) and drawn from a generic men's-trend listicle; contradicts the answer's own 'keep the sides' framing.

what_went_wrong: The draft got the buzz-vs-shave trade-off right, but the merge added a confused third option from a shaved-sides trend page and ended by endorsing longer sides, never naming the horseshoe as the look to avoid or giving one clear pick.
great_answer_would: Pick a #1-#2 buzz all over with home clippers (or a clean shave if you will keep it up), say plainly not to keep longer sides, give one-line maintenance for each, and add beard/stubble and daily scalp sunscreen.
notes: Buzz = lowest maintenance and shave every 1-3 days plus moisturiser and SPF are correct. No guard numbers, no beard advice. The three-option list contradicts the asker's 'say the best option' preference.

hallucinations.claim: "nicotine patches are not proven to be effective for quitting smoking according to the study cited [4]"
hallucinations.why: Wrong: Cochrane reviews show NRT raises quit rates by roughly 50-60%, and combination NRT more; source [4] is a Scientific American excerpt about nicotine and cognition. Discourages the aids the reference says to use.

hallucinations.claim: Withdrawal "symptoms fade within a week or two"
hallucinations.why: Reference: withdrawal peaks around days 3-7 and fades over 2-4 weeks; 'a week or two' understates it and sets the family up to expect it over too soon.

hallucinations.claim: "the Smoking Cessation group on Drugs.com has 176 members and 31 questions"
hallucinations.why: Unverifiable, irrelevant scraped page count presented as information.

what_went_wrong: Search pulled a children's family program, a Drugs.com forum and a cognition article, and the draft summarised them instead of answering; the closing line misreads [4] to claim patches don't work, the most harmful error in the batch.
great_answer_would: Give a short script for the family (no daily 'how's it going', snappiness is withdrawal, distract me, no smoking around me, no lecture if I slip), the 3-7 day peak and 2-4 week fade, a check-in cadence he chooses, and the aids (patch plus gum/lozenge, varenicline, 1-800-QUIT-NOW) with 'the patch is part of the plan'.
notes: The opening request-not-command script and 1-800-QUIT-NOW are right. The Family Check-Up, Drugs.com and Brooklyn paragraphs are padding; 'set a consequence' and 'avoid giving cigarettes as a treat' are odd for an adult quitting. Varenicline never mentioned.
